claims.text: A trace Nb addition to lightweight Al-containing high-entropy alloys promotes formation of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
The Nb-induced precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase mechanical strength.
The Nb-induced precipitates act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
Formation of the protective oxide scale improves corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Optimized processing can keep the nanoscale precipitates stable at service temperatures up to approximately 900 °C.
Thermal exposure significantly above approximately 900 °C causes precipitate coarsening.
Precipitate coarsening deteriorates the alloy's combined mechanical, corrosion, and oxidation performance.
The initial AlxCrFeNiTi-based alloy has a single-phase matrix without dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
Precise thermomechanical processing following Nb addition promotes and stabilizes nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
The relevant structural mediator is a uniform precipitate distribution at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
The precipitate-containing hierarchical microstructure permits the alloy to retain low density while achieving high strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation stability.
Relative to an otherwise identical Nb-free alloy, the Nb-modified alloy will have higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to the Nb-free alloy, the Nb-modified alloy will better resist crack initiation during cyclic saline corrosion testing.
Relative to the Nb-free alloy, the Nb-modified alloy will form a more uniform and slower-growing oxide scale at 700–900 °C.
The Nb-free baseline lacks the nanoscale precipitate network and consequently has lower strength, lower corrosion resistance, and a less protective high-temperature oxide scale.
The beneficial effects cease when an unsuitable thermal profile or exposure above the stability range coarsens the precipitates.
